claims.claim: A trained machine learning model is the learned pattern that an algorithm produces from data, saved as numbers (parameters) that map inputs to predictions for new data, without hard-coded instructions.

Training creates the model: during training the algorithm fits the model to the data, using a loss function to measure errors and adjusting the model's parameters to reduce them; before training there is an algorithm but no trained model.

Once trained, a model works as a box: inputs (features) go in and predictions (labels) come out; in the supervised case, training data that pairs feature values with known label values enables the model to predict labels for future cases.
A model is an approximation of the world, not a copy of it: machine learning is often only as good as the data it is fed, and a model's predictions can be wrong even when it seems confident.
Models are not static: a model can be updated with new data, retrained, or replaced, and machine learning systems can adjust as they accumulate experience.
Models differ in quality, and the acceptable level of quality depends on the application: accuracy that is plenty for recommending songs can be unacceptable for safety-critical uses.

Machine learning models appear in everyday products: e-commerce recommendation engines, media personalization, translation and transcription services, and weather forecasts that report probabilities such as the chance of rain.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether 'learning' is the right word for what a model does.
positions: Google Cloud and IBM describe systems that 'learn' the patterns of training data
The mechanism behind the word is parameter adjustment during an optimization process, not human-style understanding
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson keeps the familiar 'learned pattern' phrasing but explains the mechanism (the algorithm fits the model by adjusting parameters to reduce measured errors), so no magical or human-like learning is implied.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much certainty a model's output carries.
positions: The National Weather Service expresses forecasts as probabilities, such as the chance of at least 0.01 inch of rain, rather than certainties
Elements of AI warns that people can become too confident about prediction accuracy and be disappointed when it turns out worse than expected
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats predictions as estimates with uncertainty, never as guarantees, and uses the rain-probability example to make the point concrete.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How often deployed models are retrained.
positions: Google Cloud describes machine learning systems that continuously adjust and enhance themselves as they accrue experiences
Microsoft Learn frames training as a train-evaluate-refine loop, implying models are revisited rather than finished
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson claims only that models CAN be updated, retrained, or replaced, and makes no claim about how frequently real products retrain.

sourceRecords.title: What is Machine Learning? Types and uses
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21. Supports: machine learning as systems that learn and improve without being explicitly programmed; training as fitting the model to the data, with a loss function measuring the model's errors and an optimization technique adjusting the model's parameters to minimize them; applications including fraud detection, personalization and recommendations, and transcription and translation; the warning that machine learning is often only as good as the data it is fed; and systems that continuously adjust as they accrue experiences and retain new data. Facts synthesized into original lesson prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What is Machine Learning?
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21. Supports: machine learning as the subset of AI whose algorithms learn the patterns of training data and subsequently make accurate inferences about new data; models making decisions or predictions without explicit, hard-coded instructions; the central premise of optimizing performance through model training; e-commerce recommendation engines as an application; and the attribution of the term to Arthur L. Samuel's 1959 checkers paper. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Elements of AI (University of Helsinki), Chapter 4: Machine learning
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 via the chapter content served at course.elementsofai.com/4 (Gatsby page-data JSON endpoint, since the chapter is script-rendered). Supports: the warning that unless careful, one can become too confident about prediction accuracy and be disappointed when it turns out worse than expected; the quality bar depending on the application (99 percent safe cars on the streets would be unacceptable, while predicting whether you will like a new song at that accuracy may be more than enough); a regression model predicting a selling price from features such as year of construction and condition; a music-recommendation scenario; and reinforcement learning as used by a self-driving car. Lesson prose is original; the song-quality contrast is referenced conceptually.

sourceRecords.title: Explaining 'Probability of Precipitation'
